blocks: A messenger RNA vaccine contains no virus at all. It contains a recipe.
The recipe is a strand of messenger RNA, wrapped in a tiny bubble of fat, so it can slip into your cells.
Inside, your ribosomes, the cell's protein machines, read it and build one harmless piece of the virus. For COVID, that was the spike protein.
Your immune system sees that piece and learns its shape. It makes antibodies and trains T cells, without ever meeting the real virus.
Then the cell breaks the recipe down. According to the CDC, it never enters the nucleus, where your DNA is kept, and it doesn't change your DNA.
The idea had a problem for years: injected RNA set off inflammation. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman fixed it by swapping one RNA building block for a modified version.
That work, first published in two thousand five, won them the Nobel Prize in twenty twenty-three.
Vaccine recommendations depend on your age and health, and they change over time. Ask your doctor or local health authority.
